Neonates of the Grey red-backed vole weigh approximately 2 grams [Wwb = approximately 2 grams] at birth, a modest mass that reflects the altricial condition typical of many arvicoline rodents. Within the controlled environment of a laboratory colony maintained at a stable core body temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], the weaning process, marking the transition to nutritional independence, occurs at 17 days after birth [tx = 17 days after birth]. This developmental milestone aligns with the rapid postnatal growth trajectory observed in closely related species within the genus Myodes, where a brief lactation period supports a swift progression toward a juvenile state. Field studies tracking marked individuals in Hokkaido have corroborated this timeline, noting that pups begin consuming solid food alongside milk by the end of the second week. The birth mass of approximately 2 grams, while low, is typical for a species that produces relatively large litters and relies on a short gestation interval to maximize seasonal reproductive output. Such life-history traits position the Grey red-backed vole as a classic example of a fast-paced rodent life cycle within the broader context of northern temperate small mammals.

In assessing lifetime reproductive potential, captive studies have documented that individual females can give birth to litters containing between 4 and 7 pups [N_R_i = litters containing between 4 and 7 pups]. Under the stable thermal conditions of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], which approximates the species' normothermic body temperature, the maximum reproductive rate is realized through a combination of this moderate litter size and a high frequency of breeding events. Specifically, females may produce as many as 5.5 litters annually [F_R_i = 5.5 litters annually], a figure that reflects the species' capacity for a postpartum estrus and a relatively short gestation. This annual reproductive output is among the highest recorded for small rodents of comparable body size in temperate deciduous and boreal forests. The ability to sustain such a prolific breeding schedule is intimately tied to the abundance of herbaceous forage and fungal fruit bodies during the snow-free months. Litter size exhibits a degree of plasticity, with late-summer litters often falling at the lower end of the 4 to 7 pup range compared to those born during the peak spring emergence of new vegetation.

The gestation period of the Grey red-backed vole has been measured at 18.5 days [tg = 18.5 days] at the species' typical body temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], a value consistent with that reported for the closely related bank vole, Myodes glareolus, upon which the thermal measurement is based. This brief intrauterine development period is a defining feature of the species' strategy, allowing females to cram multiple litters into a single breeding season. The average wet weight at which females attain puberty has been recorded at 22.5 grams [Wwp = 22.5 grams], indicating that a substantial amount of somatic growth must occur before reproductive maturation is achieved. This weight threshold, which generally falls within a range of 22 to 23 grams, is reached after a period of intensive feeding following weaning. The time since birth at puberty for females has been established at approximately 45 days [tp = approximately 45 days], though this can vary with local food availability and population density. at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]In resource-rich habitats, some individuals may reach pubertal mass and reproductive activation in as little as 30 days, while those in marginal areas may delay beyond 60 days.

Weaning, the endpoint of direct maternal nutritional dependency, occurs when the offspring reach a wet weight of about 10 grams [Wwx = about 10 grams]. Achieving this mass requires the neonate, weighing approximately 2 grams [Wwb = approximately 2 grams] at birth, to accumulate roughly 8 grams of tissue over the course of the 17 days after birth [tx = 17 days after birth] at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. Once weaned, juveniles enter a phase of rapid somatic development, during which they must increase their body mass by more than double to reach the threshold of approximately 22.5 grams [Wwp = approximately 22.5 grams] associated with the onset of sexual maturity. The animals studied were maintained at a constant ambient temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C] to ensure comparability with the metabolic baseline. In natural populations, this post-weaning growth rate is heavily influenced by the quality of the summer forage, which is dominated by forbs, seeds, and berries. A delay in reaching the pubertal mass can push first reproduction into the following spring, underscoring the strong coupling between somatic condition and reproductive scheduling in this species.

Longevity records for the Grey red-backed vole, extrapolated from life-table data on the congener Myodes glareolus, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 3.3 years [am = approximately 3.3 years] under the laboratory conditions used to establish the metabolic reference at 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. In natural, free-living populations, few individuals survive beyond two winters, with most mortality concentrated in the first year. This relatively short lifespan is typical of small, high-fecundity mammals that invest heavily in early reproduction at the expense of somatic maintenance. The weaning mass of about 10 grams [Wwx = about 10 grams] marks the beginning of a high-risk juvenile period during which mortality from predation, especially by mustelids and avian raptors, is severe. Those individuals that survive to the pubertal milestone at approximately 45 days since birth [tp = approximately 45 days since birth] enter the breeding population with a high probability of contributing at least one litter to the next generation at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. The species' demographic strategy, combining early maturation, large litters, and a short gestation, is well-suited to the unpredictable conditions of its subarctic and montane habitats.
